title: The "I Am" Sayings
aka: I am the light of the world
I am the bread of life
lead: In John's Gospel Jesus speaks of himself with the Greek egō eimi, "I am": seven times with a picture (bread, light, door, shepherd, resurrection, way, vine) and several times with no picture at all ("before Abraham came to be, I am"). The bare form echoes the way God speaks of himself in Exodus 3:14 and Isaiah 40–55 in the Greek Old Testament.

sections.b:
The sayings with a picture are: the bread of life (John 6:35), the light of the world (John 8:12), the door for the sheep (John 10:7, 9), the good shepherd (John 10:11, 14), the resurrection and the life (John 11:25), the way, the truth and the life (John 14:6), and the true vine (John 15:1). (In John 9:5, "I am the world's light," the Greek has no egō, so it is usually not counted.) Each takes an image Israel already used for God or for God's gifts, such as manna, the pillar of fire, the shepherd and the vine, and applies it to Jesus.

The absolute sayings have no picture: "unless you believe that I am" (John 8:24), "then you will know that I am" (John 8:28), "before Abraham came to be, I am" (John 8:58), "so that when it comes to pass you will believe that I am" (John 13:19), and at the arrest, when the soldiers fall to the ground (John 18:5–8). Two more are debated: Jesus' answer to the Samaritan woman, "I am he, I who am speaking to you" (John 4:26; "he" is not in the original), and his words on the lake, "I am. Stop being afraid" (John 6:20), which can simply mean "It's me." In ordinary Greek egō eimi can just mean "it's me" (John 9:9), so context decides.

sections.b: In the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament made before Jesus, God's self-naming in Exodus 3:14 begins egō eimi ("I am the one who is"). In Isaiah God says "I am" (egō eimi) as a claim to be the only God, asking Israel to believe hoti egō eimi, "that I am," in Isaiah 43:10 (compare Isaiah 41:4; Isaiah 46:4; Deuteronomy 32:39). Most scholars think John intends this echo in the absolute sayings. Others disagree. Rudolf Bultmann traced the "I am" formula to the revelation speech of other religions of the time rather than to Isaiah, and the Jehovah's Witnesses' New World Translation renders 8:58 "I have been," reading the sayings as claims to be the one sent by God, not as the divine name. The Hebrew of Exodus 3:14, ehyeh asher ehyeh, is usually closer to "I will be who I will be."
